The Roman Republic was born in 509 BCE from the ashes of the monarchy, a pivotal moment when the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, was expelled following the infamous rape of Lucretia by his son Sextus. This event catalyzed a political revolution led by Lucius Junius Brutus and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, who established a new system of government designed to prevent the concentration of power in a single individual. The foundational structure of the Republic rested on the principle of *res publica*, or "public affair," where sovereignty theoretically belonged to the people. The executive power was vested in two consuls, elected annually by the Centuriate Assembly, who held *imperium* (the right to command armies and administer justice) but could veto each other’s actions. This dual consulship, along with the Senate—a council of former magistrates who advised on policy and controlled the treasury—created a complex system of checks and balances intended to preserve liberty and prevent tyranny, marking the beginning of a political experiment that would define Western governance for centuries.

CUDA graph replay is faster than eager kernel launching primarily because it eliminates the significant CPU-side overhead associated with the launch process. In eager execution, every kernel launch requires the CPU to validate arguments, manage stream dependencies, and communicate with the GPU driver, which can take several microseconds per launch. For applications with many small kernels, this CPU overhead can dominate execution time, leaving the GPU idle while waiting for instructions. CUDA graphs capture the entire sequence of operations—including kernels, memory copies, and dependencies—into a static data structure on the GPU. When replayed, the GPU executes this pre-compiled graph with minimal CPU intervention, drastically reducing launch latency and allowing for tighter pipelining of operations.

However, this performance gain comes with specific costs and constraints. The primary cost is the upfront overhead of capturing and instantiating the graph, which involves recording the execution sequence and optimizing it for the GPU. This makes CUDA graphs less suitable for dynamic workloads where the sequence of operations changes frequently or where kernel parameters vary significantly between runs, as re-capturing the graph for every iteration would negate the benefits.
